title: Plugin lifecycle & allocator safety probe (TensorRT + Triton + custom kernels)
content:
Purpose and scope:

This note captures a set of small, focused experiments and open tradeoffs about plugin lifecycle, GPU memory allocators, and deterministic fallback behavior when combining TensorRT engine execution, Triton server-side orchestration, and our custom kernels (XLL / custom CUDA ops). The goal: identify failure modes that cause latency spikes, OOMs, or nondeterministic behavior in production and propose short-term mitigations plus longer-term design patterns.

Summary of findings (TL;DR):
- Mixing TensorRT engines (with their own device memory layout assumptions) and custom CUDA kernels behind Triton can cause transient OOMs due to allocator fragmentation and non-returning memory pools during engine load/unload.
- KV cache (attention key/value cache) residency and eviction interacts badly with kernel hotplug: kernel unloads can invalidate cached pointer references if we use direct pointer sharding; safer to use indirection layer.
- Synchronous cold loads of TensorRT engines create 20–80 ms p99 latency spikes on RTX A6000 in our microbench; async prefetch + warmup reduced spikes to <5 ms p99 in most cases.
- Fallback policy needs two levers: fast fallback to smaller model variant and guaranteed retry to Triton-hosted CPU path; both require idempotent request tagging in the control plane.

Experiment matrix and microbench notes:

Environments:
- GPU: RTX A6000 (48 GB), Ampere-based cloud instances (A10G equivalent), dev NVLink box (2x A40).
- Runtime: Triton 23.11 branch baseline, TensorRT 8.9 engines, custom kernels compiled with CUDA 12.1.
- Allocators: 1) CUDA default (cudaMalloc/free), 2) CUB caching allocator (per-thread caching), 3) jemalloc-backed device pool shim (our experimental allocator), 4) Triton-provided pool.

Workloads:
- Short-chat streaming (max 256 tokens), heavy-batch embedding (1024 vectors), long-context generation (4096 tokens, KV cache heavy).

Key microbench numbers (representative):
- Cold engine load (synchronous): median 45 ms, p95 65 ms, p99 82 ms.
- Cold engine load (async + background warmup): median 6 ms, p95 8 ms, p99 13 ms (warm paths paved).
- KV cache footprint impact: long-context sessions increased resident memory by ~28% when using direct per-request pointer slices vs 12% with indirection + slice table.
- Eviction spike: on eviction path with CUB caching allocator we saw transient 150–180 ms stalls while freeing large pinned buffers (observed on A6000).

Root causes observed and evidence:
1) Allocator fragmentation and retention
- Caching allocators keep large blocks to reduce churn; when TensorRT engine load needs a contiguous large block, if the caching allocator has fragmented free space but has reserved large blocks elsewhere, the driver ends up calling cudaMalloc which triggers page table reorganizations and stalls.
- Evidence: NVTX traces show long gaps in kernel launch timestamps while cudaMalloc completes. Host-side stack traces point to our allocator being asked to split cached blocks.

2) Kernel unloads and dangling pointer assumptions
- Custom kernels sometimes operate on KV cache buffers passed by pointer from the serving runtime. When a TensorRT engine unloads and triggers memory compaction, GPU addresses can change (in pathological cases with our shim) causing custom kernel launches to crash or silently read stale data.
- Mitigation: add an indirection layer (global handle -> device pointer) with epoch counter. Invalidate handles on unload; kernel entry validates epoch and fails fast.

3) Synchronous warming vs race on first request
- When Triton routes a request to an instance that has not yet materialized plugin libraries and TRT engines, it currently does synchronous load in the request path. This produces unacceptable p99 spikes.
- Mitigation: add async background load with prioritized warmup queue; keep a transient single-request queue for the instant that warmup is in-flight and return a 202/queued response to downstream caller OR fast-fallback to smaller model.

4) KV cache lifecycle and sharding
- We saw that per-shard memory accounting (shard->direct pointer) is fragile across kernel updates. If a kernel patch changes buffer layout, the shard pointers become incompatible.
- Proposed approach: shard metadata contains version tag and a per-shard indirection table. On kernel upgrade, increment version and rehydrate shards incrementally.

Design proposals (short-term / recommended):
- Allocator: adopt jemalloc-backed device pool shim with explicit threshold for returning large blocks to system; tune to avoid holding blocks > 256 MB across engine transitions. Roll out as feature-flagged pilot on Dedicated clusters.
- Indirection & epochs: implement address indirection table (handle -> pointer + epoch). All custom kernel entry points must validate handle epoch. Simple fast-path: if epoch matches, read pointer; else fail fast and surface to runtime for rebind.
- Warmup: change Triton integration to support prefetch_async(engine_descriptor) as part of startup lifecycle. Provide a configurable graceful-first-request policy: queue-or-fallback.
- Fallback policy: control plane adds request metadata (request_id, is_idempotent) and runtime implements quick fallback to smaller variant on long queue/warmup. Add metrics for fallback_count, fallback_latency, fallback_success_rate.

Longer-term architecture suggestions:
- Kernel contract and ABI: define a minimal stable ABI for custom kernels (memory layout, alignment, epoch checks) and require kernels to declare compatible ABI versions in their manifest. This reduces brittle runtime assumptions.
- KV cache siloing: for Private/Dedicated tenants, run per-tenant KV cache namespaces backed by device memory segments that are pinned and cannot be moved during engine load/unload. This increases memory pressure but yields deterministic behavior for long-context customers.
- Unified allocator telemetry: extend observability to record per-engine memory high-water, fragmentation ratio (free_blocks / total_free), and allocator churn rate. Correlate these with p99 latency spikes in Console.

Operational playbook (incidents observed):
- Symptom: intermittent p99 spikes + GPU OOMs around deploy of a new TRT engine.
- Quick triage: check allocator churn metric; if > X (threshold), flip runtime flag to bypass caching allocator for hot instance and force jemalloc-ship fallback.
- If kernel crash after deploy: check epoch mismatches in logs, evict requests that reference old handle, gracefully drain instance and restart warm path.

Open questions & risks:
- Performance cost of indirection table on hot token-level paths (per-token validation) — microbench to measure overhead: expect <0.2% per-token but must validate on 8k sequence workloads.
- Backwards compatibility of ABI across 3rd-party kernels (partners). How much friction to impose?
- Memory cost of KV cache siloing (Tenant isolation vs throughput economics).

Next steps / action items:
- [Priya] Prototype indirection table + epoch check in runtime; run token-level microbench on 8k and 4k contexts by 2025-01-20.
- [Marcus] Pilot jemalloc-backed device pool on Dedicated cluster ps-3; collect allocator churn and fragmentation metrics for 2 weeks.
- [Leah] Add warmup_async API to Triton adapter and land a controlled rollout (feature flag) behind dedicated clusters; add graceful-first-request policy in control plane.
- [Alex] Draft kernel ABI doc (one-pager) and open RFC; circulate to Solutions Eng and Applied ML for partner impact.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working doc: expect fragments, TODOs, and references to in-flight PRs. Prioritize feedback on the indirection/epoch design (safety vs perf), and allocator thresholds.

Appendix: quick trace snippet (NVTX style)
- T0: request queued
- T1: Triton checks engine state -> missing -> triggers async prefetch (kicks off TRT engine load)
- T2: jemalloc pool splits, calls cudaMalloc -> stalled 24 ms
- T3: engine load completes -> kernel warmup kernels run -> KV cache bind occurs (epoch 3)
- T4: first live request hits, validates handle epoch -> success -> streaming tokens begin

End of doc.
